description: Ingito is a satellite flood map that works with no signal. Radar measures where floodwater is; the result packs into one 6.7 MB file that runs on a phone with no network, no tiles, no accounts. Tested on the 2024 Feni flood. Built for humanitarian relief teams, open to anyone who wants to use it.
summary:
In the August 2024 floods, 92% of Feni district’s mobile towers were out of service by 23 August. By the next morning, all six upazilas had lost communication. Field teams went in with no network and no current map of the water.

Radar sees through monsoon cloud and works at night, and several services already publish automated flood maps. Ingito does not compete on detection. It solves the last mile: getting that map to the person standing in the water after the network has gone, and bringing their observations back.

Ingito turns Copernicus Sentinel-1 C-band radar into a layer of new open water using the UN-SPIDER method — 21.7 km² across 1,159 patches for Feni on 21 August 2024. That figure is a lower bound, because radar sees open water only. The layer is packed with 2,293 roads, 13,230 village lanes, 927 waterways, 278 shelter points, terrain and WorldPop population estimates into a single 6.7 MB file.

The field tool is an installable web app in English and Bangla that needs no network. It answers where am I, which roads are under water, and how to reach the nearest dry shelter by road — routing only along stretches where the radar saw no water. A “Road cut” report closes a stretch and the route re-plans at once. Reports travel back out by file, by SMS, or on paper.

We have also processed NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band data for south Chattogram and NASA GPM IMERG rainfall for both areas.

Ingito is open source under Apache 2.0, with no accounts, dashboard or analytics.
details:
Team Ingito — Dhaka, Bangladesh
Challenge: Dancing with the SARs

THE PROBLEM

Monsoon cloud hides the ground from ordinary satellite cameras. Radar sees through it, and works at night. Several services already publish automated satellite flood maps, so Ingito does not compete on detection. The gap it closes is the last mile: getting that map to someone standing in the water after the network has gone, and bringing their observations back. In the August 2024 floods, 92% of Feni district’s mobile towers were out of service by 23 August, and all six upazilas had lost communication by the next morning.

HOW IT WORKS

Three parts. First, a flood layer: Sentinel-1 C-band VH radar, terrain-corrected, relative orbit 114 ascending, 9 August 2024 as baseline and 21 August 2024 as the flood pass, processed on a 20 m grid with the UN-SPIDER Recommended Practice. Otsu’s method returned 1.05, outside the plausible 1.1–2.0 range, so we used the UN-SPIDER default of 1.25. Result: 21.7 km² of new open water in 1,159 patches, 2.3% of Feni’s 929 km². Every layer carries its sensor, dates, method and limits wherever it travels.

Second, one pack file. The flood layer plus a satellite photo, two radar images, terrain, 2,293 roads, 13,230 village lanes, 927 waterways, 278 shelter points, upazila outlines and WorldPop population estimates — 6.7 MB, one file. It downloads, saves, passes phone to phone over Bluetooth or Quick Share, or gets cut down to a single upazila at about 0.5 MB.

Third, the field view: an installable web app in English and Bangla that needs no network at all. It answers where am I, which roads are under water, where the nearest shelter is, and how to reach it — routing by road and village lane using only stretches where the radar saw no water. If every route from the nearest road crosses water, it shows the one with the least, in red, with “you may need a boat.” A “Road cut” report closes the stretch it sits on and the route re-plans immediately. Two one-tap reports, Water here and Road cut, go back out as a file, as a single SMS, or on paper.

We have also built a NISAR pipeline on real NASA-ISRO L-band data for south Chattogram (30 June and 12 July 2026, track 69), sharing the same grid and method, and processed NASA GPM IMERG rainfall for both areas.

WHAT IS HONEST ABOUT IT

The 21.7 km² is a lower bound. Radar finds open water only, and misses water standing among crops, trees and houses — exactly where people live. Press reporting gives about 201 km² flooded; we detect about 11% of that, because the pass caught the flood on the day it arrived, two days before the peak. We claim no accuracy figure. “Dry” on a route means only that the radar saw no water there; it knows nothing of depth, current or broken bridges, and the app says so on screen. Shelters are unverified reference points. The NISAR area figure for south Chattogram is withheld from all material until it is validated against Sentinel-1.

WHAT WE’D BUILD NEXT

Make the NISAR layer shippable: finish validation and let the app’s labels follow each pack’s own sensor. Put rainfall on screen rather than only in the file. Extend village lanes, imagery and population to south Chattogram so routing there is as good as in Feni. Run the airplane-mode test on real phones in the field and watch first-time users without helping them. Ingito is meant to become a nonprofit, open-source tool under Apache 2.0 — no dashboard, no accounts, no analytics, by design.
